Newly hatched Jefferson salamander larvae emerge from their gelatinous egg masses after a developmental period of 15 days [ab = 15 days] when incubated at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a finding consistent with the prolonged embryonic development typical of unisexual and diploid members of the Ambystoma complex. At the moment of hatching, each larva possesses an extraordinarily small wet body mass of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the measured diameter of the deposited eggs. This minuscule birth mass places the species among the smallest neonatal salamanders within the genus, reflecting the substantial yolk reserves that are allocated to sustain the larva through its initial endotrophic, non-feeding phase before the onset of exogenous feeding following the absorption of the yolk sac.

Upon transitioning to an actively feeding aquatic larva, individuals of Ambystoma jeffersonianum experience a prolonged period of growth before reaching the metamorphic climax. Under typical thermal conditions in vernal pools, where water temperatures average 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time from hatching to the completion of metamorphosis is approximately 91.5 days from hatching , a duration that aligns with the lower end of the 2 to 4 month range reported for this species. This substantial larval period appears to be an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of their breeding habitats, allowing sufficient time for the gill-breathing tadpole to accumulate the lipid stores necessary for the dramatic morphological transformation that includes limb bud development, tail resorption, and the transition to a terrestrial juvenile form.

Following metamorphosis, the resulting terrestrial juvenile enters a sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual maturation of the reproductive system. For females, the interval between completing metamorphosis and attaining puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, spans approximately 671 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 671 days following metamorphosis] when maintained at an environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This delay of nearly two years before reproductive viability reflects the substantial energetic demands of reaching the critical body size required for successful first egg deposition in the subsequent breeding season. During this period, the growing juvenile actively forages on forest-floor invertebrates to meet the elevated metabolic costs of tissue synthesis and fat storage.

Reproductively mature females of Ambystoma jeffersonianum eventually attain a maximum adult wet body mass of 7.06 grams [Wwi = 7.06 grams], a value that distinguishes them from the slightly smaller males of the species and represents the ultimate body size achieved under optimal habitat conditions. This asymptotic mass is associated with a relatively slow life history, as the maximum recorded longevity in the wild is approximately 3,723 days [am = approximately 3,723 days], or just over a decade, at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Such an extended lifespan, which was inferred from mark-recapture studies of the closely related congener Ambystoma gracile, allows females multiple reproductive opportunities across consecutive springs, thereby compensating for the relatively modest annual reproductive output.

The basal metabolic rate of a resting adult Jefferson salamander, measured through respirometry trials at the species' preferred active temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is 0.0054 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0054 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the low-energy lifestyle typical of ambystomatid salamanders. This reduced metabolic demand supports a life history strategy in which females produce relatively few offspring per year; field observations indicate that a gravid female deposits approximately 250 eggs per season [Ri = approximately 250 eggs per season], with a single annual breeding event each year [F_R_i = single annual breeding event each year], giving a maximum annual reproductive output of 250 eggs per year [Ri = 250 eggs per year] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This modest reproductive rate, which is consistent with the maximum attainable output for the species, contrasts sharply with the high fecundity of many anuran amphibians and underscores the importance of adult survival and iteroparity in maintaining stable population dynamics.

An additional noteworthy aspect of the life history of the Jefferson salamander relates to the ecological context of its vernal pool breeding habitat, where the timing of oviposition and subsequent larval development are tightly coupled to seasonal hydroperiods. The species' preference for cool, fishless temporary ponds means that larvae must complete metamorphosis before the pools dry in early summer, a constraint that may explain the relatively narrow range of variation in the duration of the larval stage. Comparisons with other members of the Ambystoma genus, such as the spotted salamander (Ambystoma maculatum), reveal that A. jeffersonianum exhibits a somewhat faster developmental rate under equivalent thermal regimes, likely reflecting selection pressures imposed by the shorter hydroperiod of the pools it typically occupies. Understanding these interspecific differences in larval duration and its relationship to environmental temperature is critical for predicting how changing climate patterns might affect the recruitment success and long-term persistence of this species in its naturally fragmented landscape.
